generalfeedback.text:
Worked Solution

A. To find the derivative of the function \(f(x) = {@func@}\) at a specific point, \(x = {@lim_point@}\), we can use the limit definition of a derivative (the difference quotient).

The formula for finding the derivative of a function \(f(x)\) at a point \(x = a\) is given by:

\( \displaystyle f'(a) = \lim_{h \to 0} \frac{f(a + h) - f(a)}{h}\)

In this case, we want to find \( \displaystyle f'({@lim_point@})\), so \(a = {@lim_point@}\). Therefore, we have:

\( \displaystyle f'({@lim_point@}) = \lim_{h \to 0} \frac{f({@lim_point@} + h) - f({@lim_point@})}{h}\)

Now, plug in the function \(f(x) = {@func@}\):

\( \displaystyle f'({@lim_point@}) = \lim_{h \to 0} \frac{{@func_coeff@}({@lim_point@} + h)^{@func_power@} - {@func_coeff@}({@lim_point@})^{@func_power@}}{h}\)

Now, simplify the expression inside the limit:

\( \begin{align*} \displaystyle f'({@lim_point@}) &= \lim_{h \to 0} \frac{{@func_coeff@}({@lim_point@} + h)^{@func_power@} -{@num_right@}}{h} \\ &= \lim_{h \to 0} \frac{{@func_coeff@}({@num_left@}) - {@num_right@}}{h} \\ &= \lim_{h \to 0} \frac{{@num_left1@} - {@num_right@}}{h} \\ &= \lim_{h \to 0} \frac{{@func_num@}}{h} \\ &= \lim_{h \to 0} \frac{{@func_num_simp@}}{h} \\ &= \lim_{h \to 0} {@func_num_simp1@} \end{align*} \)

Now, you can evaluate the limit as \(h\) approaches \(0\):

\(\displaystyle f'({@lim_point@}) = {@correct_limit@} \)

B. So, the exact limit of \( \displaystyle f'({@lim_point@}) = {@correct_limit@}\).

This is the derivative of the function \( \displaystyle f(x) = {@func@}\) at \(x = {@lim_point@}\), as found using the limit definition of a derivative.

C. To find the gradient (\(m\)) of the tangent to the graph of \(f(x) = {@func@}\) when \(x = {@lim_point@}\), we can use the derivative of the function \(f(x)\) at that point.

The gradient of the tangent line at a specific point is equal to the value of the derivative of the function at that point.

First, we find the derivative of \(f(x)\) with respect to \(x\):

\( \displaystyle \begin{align*} f'(x) &= \frac{d}{dx}({@func@}) = {@df@} \\ f'({@lim_point@}) &= {@m@} \\ m &= f'({@lim_point@}) = {@m@} \end{align*}\)

D. We already have \(m = {@m@}\), and we can use the point \(({@lim_point@}, f({@lim_point@}))\) on the graph of \(f(x)\) to find \(c\).

Plug \(x = {@lim_point@}\) into the original function to find \(f({@lim_point@})\):

\(f({@lim_point@}) = {@func_coeff@} ({@lim_point@}^{@func_power@})= {@fx_at_lim_point@}\)

Now, you have a point \(({@lim_point@}, {@fx_at_lim_point@})\) and the gradient \(m = {@m@}\). Plug these values into the equation \(y = mx + c\) and solve for \(c\):

\( \displaystyle \begin{align*} {@fx_at_lim_point@} &= ({@m@} \times {@lim_point@}) + c \\ {@fx_at_lim_point@} &= {@m*lim_point@} + c \\ c &= {@fx_at_lim_point@} - {@m*lim_point@} \\ &= {@c@} \end{align*}\)

So, the equation of the tangent to the graph of \(f(x) = {@func@}\) when \(x = {@lim_point@}\) is:

\( \qquad y = {@tangent_line@}\)
